description: Axons that connect the two halves of the nervous system must cross the midline exactly once, and SLIT–ROBO signalling is the switch that makes a single crossing possible. Before crossing, commissural axons are drawn to the floor plate by Netrin-1 acting on the DCC receptor, while ROBO3 dampens the repulsive receptors ROBO1 and ROBO2 so that midline-derived SLIT1, SLIT2 and SLIT3 are ignored; the secreted cue NELL2, read through ROBO3, keeps growth cones steered toward the midline from the motor column side. Once inside the floor plate, SLIT-bound ROBO associates with DCC and silences the attractive netrin response, ROBO3 is downregulated and alternatively spliced, and the axon is expelled contralaterally and barred from re-crossing. SRC-family kinase activity couples these receptors to cytoskeletal remodelling. Loss of ROBO3 underlies horizontal gaze palsy with progressive scoliosis, in which hindbrain axons fail to cross.

Sema4D binding to plexin-B1 reshapes the actin cytoskeleton, driving endothelial cell migration in angiogenesis while causing growth cones of responding neurons to collapse and retract, so the same ligand steers vessel and axon guidance in opposite directions depending on context. Plexin-B1 acts as a receptor whose cytoplasmic tail recruits the RhoA-specific exchange factors ARHGEF11 and ARHGEF12 and binds the small GTPase RND1, and in endothelium its association with ERBB2 couples receptor occupancy to RhoA, RhoB and RhoC activation. Active RhoA engages ROCK1 and ROCK2, which phosphorylate myosin regulatory light chains such as MYL9 and MYL12B and activate LIM kinases; the resulting non-muscle myosin II contractility builds stress fibres, stabilizes focal adhesions and integrin-mediated adhesion in migrating cells, or in neurons collapses the peripheral actin network. This branch is Rho-dependent and distinct from the R-Ras-directed arm of plexin signalling.

Axon guidance receptors of the ROBO family steer growing axons away from midline Slit sources, and their cytoplasmic tails can be coupled to local kinase and phosphatase activity through a scaffold. The binding of AKAP5 to ROBO2 and to the ROBO3.1 isoform brings protein kinase A, protein kinase C and the calcium/calmodulin-dependent phosphatase calcineurin into the immediate vicinity of the receptor, so that guidance signalling is read out alongside cAMP and calcium cues rather than in isolation. PKC recruited in this way phosphorylates ROBO3.1. Such anchoring is the general strategy AKAP proteins use to confine broadly acting kinases to defined membrane microdomains, and in neurons it links receptor engagement at the growth cone to cytoskeletal remodelling and decisions about midline crossing. The downstream consequences of the ROBO-AKAP5 interaction itself remain undefined, with the complex demonstrated in brain tissue.

CHL1, a close homolog of L1, is an immunoglobulin-superfamily adhesion receptor on subsets of neurons and glia that supports neuronal survival, neurite extension and the steering of growing axons. Unlike other L1 family members it does not bind itself homophilically, so its signalling depends on partners: contactin-6 in trans, beta1-containing integrin heterodimers engaged through RGD and DGEA motifs in its Ig domains, and neuropilin-1, through which it converts secreted Semaphorin-3A into a repulsive turning or collapse response in the growth cone. Its cytoplasmic tail contacts ankyrin, linking adhesion to the spectrin cytoskeleton, and a chaperone interaction is also part of its handling at the membrane. These contacts translate extracellular guidance cues into cytoskeletal change during nervous system wiring, and CHL1 loss is associated with abnormal axon targeting and neurodevelopmental deficits.

Growth cones advance by gripping the substrate at the front and letting go at the back, and the recycling of the adhesion molecule L1 is how that asymmetry is maintained. L1CAM links immobile extracellular ligands to retrograde actin flow through ERM proteins such as ezrin, radixin and moesin, so that cytoskeletal movement is converted into forward traction; without this, axon outgrowth and neuronal migration fail, and L1CAM mutations cause X-linked hydrocephalus and corpus callosum agenesis. A tyrosine-based sorting motif in the L1 cytoplasmic tail is read by the AP-2 clathrin adaptor only when unphosphorylated, so SRC-mediated phosphorylation retains L1 at the peripheral membrane while dephosphorylation at the central domain licenses clathrin- and dynamin-dependent endocytosis. Internalized L1 is then carried anterogradely along microtubules, with kinesin motors and shootin-1, back to the leading edge for reuse.

Growing axons are steered by the same guidance cue in opposite directions depending on which receptor they display, and netrin-mediated repulsion is the arm that turns netrin-1 into a turning-away signal. It shapes the trajectories of commissural and other projecting neurons, and the same receptors act in vascular patterning and as regulators of cell survival, since UNC5 family members are dependence receptors that trigger death when unoccupied by ligand. Netrin binding to UNC5A-D promotes phosphorylation within the receptor's ZU-5 domain, with Src-family kinase activity and the phosphatase SHP2 relaying the signal to the actin cytoskeleton of the growth cone. Long-range repulsion additionally requires cooperation with DCC, whose cytoplasmic domain pairs with UNC5, whereas UNC5 alone suffices at short range. Loss of this steering causes misrouted commissures and defective neural wiring.

DSCAM and its paralogue DSCAML1 are immunoglobulin-superfamily adhesion receptors on the neuronal surface, and their interactions guide growing axons and set the spacing of neurites and cell bodies in the developing nervous system. Both engage in homophilic binding, cell to cell, which mediates self-recognition and the repulsion that keeps sister branches and like neurons from overlapping; loss of this activity disrupts dendritic tiling and retinal mosaic arrangement. DSCAM also cooperates with the netrin receptor DCC in responding to the secreted guidance cue netrin-1, linking adhesive contact to the attractive turning of commissural axons at the midline. The gene lies in the chromosome 21 region associated with Down syndrome, though a direct causal contribution remains unproven. Overall this is cell-surface adhesion feeding into axon pathfinding, lamina targeting and the wiring precision of neural circuits.

NrCAM is an L1-family adhesion receptor that helps axons find their targets and helps assemble the specialized membrane domains of myelinated nerve, including the node of Ranvier; it is also needed for normal eye development, and its loss is associated with axon guidance and lens defects. Its interactions fall into three groups. Through a cytoplasmic ankyrin-binding segment it couples the adhesive surface to the spectrin-based cytoskeleton, clustering receptors at nodes. A C-terminal PDZ-binding motif engages membrane-associated guanylate kinase scaffolds of the SAP97/SAP102/PSD-95 family, linking NrCAM into postsynaptic and submembrane protein networks. Extracellularly it binds the GPI-anchored contactin axonin-1/TAG-1 to promote neurite outgrowth, and partners with neuropilin-2 in the receptor complex that converts class 3 semaphorin cues into repulsive axon turning. Together these contacts make NrCAM a bridge between guidance signalling and cytoskeletal organisation.

L1 family adhesion molecules are anchored to the underlying membrane skeleton through ankyrins, and this link determines where adhesion and excitability machinery sit on a neuron's surface. Ankyrin-G, ankyrin-B and ankyrin-R bind the cytoplasmic tails of L1CAM, neurofascin and NrCAM and tether them, together with voltage-gated sodium channels and KCNQ2/KCNQ3 potassium channels, to spectrin-actin networks built from alpha and beta spectrins. Coupling restrains lateral diffusion in the plasma membrane and strengthens homophilic adhesion, which in turn supports axon guidance, branching and synaptogenesis of cortical inhibitory neurons, and concentrates sodium channels at axon initial segments and nodes of Ranvier so that action potentials initiate and propagate reliably. Mutations in L1CAM cause X-linked hydrocephalus and spastic paraplegia, while ankyrin and channel defects underlie epilepsy, cardiac arrhythmia and hereditary spherocytosis.

Semaphorins are guidance cues that tell migrating cells and growing axons where not to go, and plexins are their principal receptors; beyond the canonical class 3 to plexin-A route, a broad set of other semaphorin interactions couples transmembrane and GPI-anchored semaphorins to plexins of the A, B, C and D subfamilies and to non-plexin partners. These contacts steer axon repulsion and fasciculation, vascular patterning, bone remodelling and immune cell behaviour. Specificity comes from the receptor combination: SEMA4D acting through CD72 on B cells, SEMA4A and SEMA6 family members engaging plexin-A receptors, SEMA7A signalling through integrin alpha1/beta1 rather than a plexin, and SEMA6D working with the TREM2-TYROBP adaptor pair in myeloid cells. SEMA3E-PLXND1 restricts endothelial sprouting. Loss of these cues produces miswired circuits, disordered vessel branching and altered immune activation.

Guidance cues steer growing axons and restrain cell motility by reshaping the actin cytoskeleton, and this branch of SLIT-ROBO signalling does so by raising RHOA activity. When SLIT2 binds the ROBO1 receptor, the receptor engages the unconventional myosin MYO9B and blocks its RHOA GTPase-activating function; with GTP hydrolysis on RHOA suppressed, the active GTP-bound pool rises. The consequence is ROCK activation and phosphorylation of the myosin regulatory light chain, generating the actomyosin contractility that cranial motor neuron axons require to follow SLIT cues correctly. The same output limits cell migration and invasion, and loss of this restraint has been linked to increased invasiveness of lung cancer cells. It illustrates how a receptor can raise small GTPase activity by inhibiting an inhibitor rather than recruiting an exchange factor.

Neurofascin is an L1-family immunoglobulin adhesion molecule whose interactions organize specialized axonal membrane domains, and this adhesive biology is what allows nodes of Ranvier and axo-glial junctions to form and hold together so that saltatory conduction works. Distinct isoforms act on either side of the junction: the neuronal 186 kDa form clusters at nodes with NrCAM and is anchored to the spectrin-based cytoskeleton through ankyrin, while the glial 155 kDa form works with contactin and its associated protein CNTNAP1 to build the paranodal septate-like junction with the myelinating cell. A C-terminal class I PDZ-binding motif recruits syntenin-1, linking adhesion to intracellular scaffolding and trafficking, and the presence of doublecortin reflects the roles these contacts play in axon subcellular targeting, neurite outgrowth and synapse formation during neural development. Disruption of these contacts causes paranodal disorganization and conduction failure, and neurofascin is an autoantigen in inflammatory neuropathy.

Cortical neurons acquire their input capacity by elaborating dendritic arbors, and this branching programme sets how many synapses a pyramidal cell can receive and therefore how cortical circuits are wired. The same secreted guidance cue family that repels growing axons is reused here for a constructive purpose: SLIT1 binds the transmembrane receptors ROBO1 and ROBO2 on cortical dendrites and, instead of causing retraction, promotes the formation of new branch points. The cytoplasmic adaptor NCK2 couples activated ROBO to the actin regulatory machinery and is required for the branching response, illustrating how the interpretation of a guidance signal depends on which effector is engaged in which compartment. Disturbed regulation of cortical dendrite branching yields simplified arbors and altered connectivity of the kind associated with neurodevelopmental and intellectual disability phenotypes, placing this signalling within cytoskeletal control of neuronal morphogenesis.

Growing axons steer by reading guidance cues, and netrin-1 is one of the strongest attractants for commissural axons crossing the midline of the developing spinal cord. Whether a growth cone turns toward or away from netrin depends on the second messengers it generates, so this signalling sets the wiring of long-range connections; loss of the pathway leaves axons unable to reach their targets, and the netrin receptor DCC is also mutated in congenital mirror movements and corpus callosum agenesis. Netrin binding to DCC engages phospholipase C gamma, aided by phosphatidylinositol transfer, to produce IP3 and diacylglycerol. IP3 releases calcium from endoplasmic reticulum stores while diacylglycerol directly gates TRPC3 and TRPC6; store depletion recruits other TRPC channels, and the resulting calcium influx at the growth cone, tuned by cyclic nucleotide levels, determines attraction versus repulsion.

EphB receptors bound by membrane-anchored ephrin-B ligands on a neighbouring cell signal into the receptor-bearing neuron, and this forward signalling shapes dendritic spines during central nervous system development. It converts contact between cells into synapse formation: filopodia become motile, find a partner, shorten, and mature into mushroom-shaped spines, with NMDA receptor subunits recruited to the new postsynaptic site. The output is cytoskeletal. Clustered receptors engage Src-family kinases and focal adhesion kinase, and recruit guanine nucleotide exchange factors such as intersectin and kalirin that load CDC42 and RAC1; these drive Arp2/3-dependent actin branching and PAK signalling, while a parallel RHOA-ROCK-LIMK arm phosphorylates cofilin to stabilise existing filaments. Loss of this signalling leaves spines immature and synapses sparse, and the same receptors guide axons and set tissue boundaries elsewhere.

Growing axons are steered as much by being pushed away as by being pulled, and Sema3A repulsion is the classic example: the secreted cue binds neuropilin-1, which pairs with a plexin-A family receptor to transduce the signal and collapse the growth cone. The route described here works by switching off substrate adhesion, so a neurite loses traction on the extracellular matrix and turns away; the same logic restrains migration of non-neuronal cells. Plexin GAP activity toward R-Ras lowers integrin affinity for ligand, while Rnd1 and Rac1 gate plexin activation and cytoskeletal remodelling, FARP2 acts as a guanine nucleotide exchange factor, and Src-family and Fes kinases relay phosphorylation. Talin and the lipid kinase PIP5K1C link the output to focal adhesion assembly. Disrupting it misroutes axons and disturbs wiring of the peripheral and central nervous systems.

Semaphorin 4D acting through plexin-B1 tells a cell to let go and turn away, converting an extracellular guidance cue into loss of integrin-mediated adhesion and collapse of the leading edge. This repulsive signalling shapes axon guidance and growth cone steering, and the same receptor pair is co-opted in vascular and tumour settings, where plexin-B1 partners with the receptor tyrosine kinase MET. Ligand binding allows Rnd1 to engage plexin-B1 and switch on its intracellular GTPase-activating domain, which lowers active R-Ras; the resulting drop in PI3K and Akt output relieves inhibition of GSK-3beta, which phosphorylates and inactivates the microtubule assembly factor CRMP2. In parallel, recruitment of p190RhoGAP transiently reduces RhoA-GTP, and Rac1 activity is redirected, so that actin and microtubule dynamics at the periphery favour retraction rather than protrusion.

SLIT ligands and their ROBO receptors steer growing axons away from inappropriate territory, most visibly at the midline, and set the paths of commissural projections, so the amount of each protein a neuron displays at a given moment determines how it responds to guidance cues. This pathway covers how those levels are set, at every step from gene to functional receptor. LIM-homeodomain factors such as LHX2, LHX3, LHX4, LHX9 and ISL1, together with HOXA2, drive ROBO and SLIT transcription in a cell-type-dependent way; the RNA-binding protein MSI1 boosts translation of ROBO3 mRNA, with ribosomal subunits, cap-binding and nonsense-mediated decay components supplying the translational machinery. Protein abundance is then tuned by ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation, opposed by the deubiquitinase USP33 which stabilises ROBO1, while dystroglycan and a collagen IV chain anchor secreted SLITs where they are needed. Misregulation contributes to axon guidance defects and to invasive behaviour in cancer.

Ephrin signaling is bidirectional: when a B-type ephrin on one cell meets an EPH receptor on another, the receptor transmits a forward signal and the ligand itself transmits a reverse signal back into its own cell. This two-way readout of cell-cell contact steers growth cones, sets tissue boundaries, and shapes dendritic spines; loss of it misroutes corpus callosum and retinal axons and, for ephrin-B1, produces craniofrontonasal developmental defects. Reverse signaling works two ways. Src-family kinases including FYN and SRC phosphorylate conserved tyrosines on the ephrin cytoplasmic tail, recruiting the adaptor NCK2 and, through GIT1, ARHGEF7 and PAK kinases, converting the contact into RAC1-dependent actin and myosin light chain remodeling. Alternatively the C-terminal PDZ-binding motif engages scaffolds such as syntenin, coupling adhesion to junctional and synaptic organization rather than to kinase output.

Growing axons decide whether to cross the midline, and RAC1 activation is how a repulsive guidance cue is converted into remodelling of the actin cytoskeleton at the growth cone. A low level of RAC1 activity sustains axon outgrowth, so the pathway is less an on-off switch than a set point that shapes where a growth cone advances and where it turns away; loss of this control produces midline crossing errors and mispatterned commissural tracts. SLIT2 binding to the ROBO1 receptor exposes cytoplasmic motifs that recruit the adaptors NCK1 or NCK2, which bring the dual-specificity exchange factors SOS1 and SOS2 to the membrane, where they load GTP onto RAC1. Active RAC1 then engages PAK family serine/threonine kinases, linking receptor occupancy to actin and adhesion dynamics, and placing this repulsion step within broader Rho-family control of cell shape and motility.

Growing axons are steered as much by repulsion as by attraction, and Sema3A is one of the classic repellents: growth cones that meet it collapse and turn away, which is how sensory and cortical projections are kept out of inappropriate territory and how peripheral nerve and dendrite patterning is set. Signal reception requires neuropilin-1 as the ligand-binding subunit together with a plexin-A family receptor, and the PAK-dependent arm of the response converts that binding into actin disassembly. Rac1 recruited to the receptor complex activates group I PAK kinases, which phosphorylate LIMK1; LIMK1 in turn phosphorylates cofilin, blocking its actin-severing and depolymerising activity and remodelling filaments in the collapsing growth cone. Src-family and Fes kinases and HSP90 chaperones support signal transmission. Loss of this route leaves axons insensitive to a major guidance cue and mistargeted.

Contact between an EPH receptor-bearing cell and an ephrin-bearing cell usually ends in withdrawal rather than sticking, and this contact-dependent repulsion is how growth cones, axon branches and migrating cells are steered away from inappropriate territory. It patterns retinotopic maps, guides commissural and corticospinal axons, keeps tissue boundaries sharp, and its loss produces mis-wired projections and disordered cell segregation. Because the trans-cellular EPH-ephrin interaction is of high affinity, adhesion must be actively dismantled: transmembrane and secreted proteases including ADAM10 and matrix metalloproteinases cleave the ligand or receptor, gamma-secretase components process the remaining stub, and clathrin- and AP-2-dependent endocytosis with dynamin internalises intact receptor-ligand complexes. Src-family kinases transmit the signal, while RAC1 activated through TIAM1 and VAV exchange factors drives the actin remodelling that collapses the growth cone and retracts the membrane.

The adhesion molecule L1CAM does more than glue neurons together: it acts as a receptor that converts contact with the extracellular environment into decisions about axon growth, guidance and cell migration. This signalling underlies neurite extension and pathfinding during nervous system development, and loss-of-function mutations in L1CAM cause X-linked hydrocephalus and related syndromes with corticospinal tract and corpus callosum defects. On the cell surface L1 partners with beta1- and beta3-containing integrins, triggering Src-family kinase activity, the exchange factor VAV2, RAC1 and PAK1, and thence the MEK1/2-ERK1/2 cascade that drives motility and outgrowth. L1 also serves as an obligate co-receptor with neuropilin-1 for semaphorin 3A-induced growth cone collapse, so the same molecule can mediate repulsion or, through homophilic trans binding, attraction. Association with FGFR1 and casein kinase 2 phosphorylation add further layers of control.

Growing axons steer by retracting from repellent cues, and the collapsin response mediator proteins are the cytosolic step that converts one such cue, Sema3A, into a change in the growth cone cytoskeleton. Sema3A binds a receptor made of neuropilin-1 together with a plexin-A, and the plexin's cytoplasmic tail holds CRMP family members (CRMP1 and the related DPYSL proteins) close to the kinases that modify them. Sequential phosphorylation by Fyn-recruited Cdk5 with its neuronal activator p35, by Fes, and by GSK3beta strips CRMPs of their ability to bind tubulin heterodimers, so microtubule assembly stalls and F-actin depolymerises, collapsing the growth cone and turning the axon away. This axon guidance and neuronal differentiation machinery patterns cortical and sensory projections, and CRMP phosphorylation by the same kinases is a recurring feature of neurodegenerative and regenerative failure in injured nerves.

Growing axons steer by retreating from repulsive cues, and ephrin-A binding to EPHA receptors is one of the main signals that makes a growth cone collapse and pull back. This repulsion keeps axons out of territories rich in ephrin-A and is how topographic maps, such as the retinal projection onto the superior colliculus, acquire their graded order; losing it produces mistargeted projections. Ligand engagement clusters EPHA receptors and recruits Src-family kinases, which phosphorylate and switch the exchange factor ephexin (NGEF) toward RHOA activation while Cdc42 and Rac1 signalling falls. Active RHOA drives ROCK1 and ROCK2 to phosphorylate myosin regulatory light chains, and non-muscle myosin II contracts the actin network faster than it can extend. The net shift from protrusion to contraction disassembles filopodia and lamellipodia, converting a receptor-ligand contact into directed axon retraction.

Growing axons steer toward sources of netrin-1, and DCC is the receptor that converts that gradient into attraction, guiding commissural axons across the midline and wiring the two halves of the nervous system together. Loss of this attractive signalling leaves midline crossing incomplete, as seen in congenital mirror movements and agenesis of the corpus callosum. DCC itself has no catalytic activity; instead the kinases FAK, Src and Fyn associate with its cytoplasmic tail and, on netrin binding, phosphorylate it and recruit adaptors such as NCK1 and DOCK1. These feed the Rho-family GTPases RAC1 and CDC42 and the exchange factor TRIO, while WASL and the actin-binding ABLIM proteins remodel filaments in the growth cone. The output is asymmetric actin polymerisation and filopodial extension on the netrin-facing side, turning a diffusible cue into directed growth-cone motility.

Growing axons steer by retracting from repellent cues, and this branch of SLIT–ROBO signalling provides the switch that does it: inactivation of CDC42 and RAC1 collapses the actin-based protrusions at the leading edge of a growth cone. Repulsive guidance of commissural and cortical axons, midline crossing decisions, and the positioning of neurons during cortical development all depend on it, and disruption of SRGAP-family genes is associated with intellectual disability and defective neuronal migration. Mechanistically, SLIT2 binding to ROBO1 exposes a cytoplasmic motif that recruits SLIT/ROBO-specific GAPs, SRGAP1–3 and the Vilse/CrossGAP orthologue ARHGAP39, which stimulate GTP hydrolysis on CDC42 and RAC1 and so return these small GTPases to their inactive GDP-bound state. Lowering Rho GTPase activity withdraws the filopodial and lamellipodial drive, linking a receptor at the membrane to cytoskeletal remodelling and directed motility.

Growing axons are steered away from the midline when the secreted cue SLIT binds ROBO receptors, and the ABL kinases sit at the point where that repellent signal is converted into cytoskeletal change. This determines whether commissural axons cross the midline once or recross inappropriately, and the same receptor-kinase axis is reused in epithelial polarity and in tumour cell migration. ABL1 and ABL2 act in two directions at once: they phosphorylate effectors that reorganise the growth cone, and they phosphorylate ROBO1 itself, tuning how sensitive the receptor remains to further SLIT. Their partners span both major cytoskeletal systems, with the cyclase-associated proteins CAP1 and CAP2 governing actin filament turnover and CLASP1/CLASP2 acting on microtubule plus ends, so filopodial collapse and microtubule behaviour are coordinated rather than controlled separately.
